items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Curtis Fuller and Louis Hayes and … they'd all gone on to New York before I even got to visit the clubs in New York.

ctx.x: Because everybody else was a few years older. Roland was like that one year too late … for …
Yeah. And Paul, and Kenny Burrell, Yusef Lateef, and Curtis …Curtis Fuller and Louis Hayes and … they'd all gone on to New York before I even got to visit the clubs in New York.
Okay. So '55, you're off to Eastman, you do your first year, you come back, you work summers …

items.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So they changed and got me in there. Ron Carter, and all those guys… They were really tight, they still are.

ctx.x: Yeah. Great player and he was from Ohio. You wanted to know about the connection… Anyways, we started playing and he would arrange little things with Clifford Brown (scats melody) “Ronnie Speaks” and all that. He was playing that stuff at the and all over that chump player. He and Joe and I had a unique thing in Detroit and Barry sort of resent that because he wanted me because Kiani didn't play the parts quite like that. He had a sluggish way of playing it; he was playing the part, but he was always behind the…

a very good player. His lines were impeccable, you know? His playing lines… He wrote some beautiful sextet arrangements, you know? If you go back and listen to "Lotus Flower” those pretty things that Kenny Dorham wrote, have you ever heard it? He did it with JJ and Cecil. It goes like this (sings the head of the song). That's pretty music. See, I'm a romanticist. I like pretty melodies and stuff like that. Kenny Dorham gave this kind of thoughts to me. But, Golson's repertoire has been repeated so much to me.…
group together and we brought in McCoy Tyner, who Benny knew from Philadelphia. It worked like a glove.
